Bars
barz
n. pl. (rods used to fasten a gate or bind a frame; figuratively, fixed limits; rendering Hebrew beriach)
From Old French barre, of uncertain origin. Hebrew beriach is from barach, to flee or pass through — a bar is what stops the passing through, whether shot across a gate or run through the rings of a frame.

Biblical Definition

Bars in Scripture hold things together and hold things out. In the tabernacle they are structural: “thou shalt make bars of shittim wood; five for the boards of the one side of the tabernacle” (Exodus 26:26) — the boards stood upright and the bars ran through their rings, so that a tent of separate planks became one house. God's dwelling was engineered for unity, and the parts were held by what passed through them all. In a city, bars are security, and their strengthening is a blessing: “For he hath strengthened the bars of thy gates; he hath blessed thy children within thee” (Psalm 147:13). The two clauses belong together — safe gates and blessed children, defence and family in one breath. Nehemiah's rebuilders set them in place gate by gate: they “laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof” (Nehemiah 3:3), a verse repeated like a refrain through that chapter as ordinary men finished ordinary sections. And Jonah, from the fish's belly, uses the word for the shut world of the dead: “the earth with her bars was about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O LORD my God” (Jonah 2:6). The bars were for ever, and were opened; the type our Lord applied to himself.

Webster 1828 Definition

Rods that fasten or bind. In the tabernacle they make many boards one house; in a city they are a blessing set beside blessed children; in Jonah they are the everlasting bars of the grave, and they opened.

expand to see more

BAR, n. [Fr. barre.] A piece of wood, iron or other solid matter, long in proportion to its diameter, used for various purposes, but especially for a hindrance or obstruction.

2. Any obstacle which obstructs, hinders or defends; an obstruction; a fortification.

3. The bar of a court; the place where prisoners are stationed.

4. A bank of sand, gravel or earth, forming a shoal at the mouth of a river or harbor.

5. In Scripture, bars of iron and brass, the fastenings of gates; I will break in pieces the gates of brass, Is. 45.

Key Scripture

Exodus 26:26 — "And thou shalt make bars of shittim wood; five for the boards of the one side of the tabernacle,"

Psalm 147:13 — "For he hath strengthened the bars of thy gates; he hath blessed thy children within thee."

Nehemiah 3:3 — "But the fish gate did the sons of Hassenaah build, who also laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof."

Jonah 2:6 — "I went down to the bottoms of the mountains; the earth with her bars was about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O LORD my God."

Modern Corruption

Limits are treated as an insult to the self, so that every bar is read as a restriction to be broken — while Scripture makes bars a blessing, a structure, and the mark of a world God has bounded.

expand to see more

The instinct that all boundaries are oppressive would have to call Psalm 147:13 a curse. There the strengthened bars of the gates and the blessed children within are one thought: without the bars the children are not safe, and a city with nothing shut is not free but exposed. Scripture is unembarrassed about limits because it holds that God set them — to the sea he said hitherto shalt thou come, but no further, and the same speech that bounds the ocean bounds a man's days and a nation's borders. Bars in the tabernacle make the same point constructively: the boards did not lose anything by being bound; they became a dwelling place for God, which no single plank could be.

The principle to recover is Jonah's. He describes bars that were for ever — the settled, unbreakable enclosure of death — and in the same sentence says God brought up his life from corruption. Our Lord took Jonah's three days as the sign of his own burial, and the New Testament announces that he has the keys of hell and of death (Revelation 1:18). The one bar that could not be broken from inside was broken from outside, which is why the church has never been able to treat the grave as final and has always buried its dead in hope.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew beriach is a bar or bolt, from barach, to pass through — both the bar run through rings and the bolt shot across a gate.

expand to see more

Hebrew beriach (H1280) — a bar, a bolt; the tabernacle bars and the bars of a city gate.

Hebrew barach (H1272) — to flee, to pass through; the root, from the bar that runs through the boards.

Hebrew manul (H4514) — a lock or bolt; the locks set with the bars in Nehemiah 3:3.

Hebrew metil (H4300) — a bar or rod of metal; the bars of iron and brass.

Greek mochlos — a bar or bolt; the Septuagint term where the Hebrew has beriach.

Usage

"Of the bars that made the tabernacle one: thou shalt make bars of shittim wood (Exodus 26:26)."

"Of bars as a blessing on a city: he hath strengthened the bars of thy gates (Psalm 147:13)."

"Of the bars of the grave broken: the earth with her bars was about me for ever (Jonah 2:6)."
